title: Evidence of Local Corrosion of Bimetallic Cu−Sn Catalysts and Its Effects on the Selectivity of Electrochemical CO2 Reduction
abstract: The electrochemical carbon dioxide (CO2) reduction is a promising method for carbon recycling. Bimetallic catalysts have been extensively developed for the selective production of carbon monoxide (CO) and formate (HCOOH), while efforts to understand the change in structure and composition under reaction conditions have been limited. Here, we provided experimental evidence for the local corrosion phenomenon of bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts through the patterning of the Sn layer on Cu foil (Cu/p-Sn). The surface composition and morphology of Cu/p-Sn 3 nm catalysts spontaneously changed during the reaction in CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte. The Sn patterns became thinner, and the Sn elements were migrated to the outside of the patterns. Consequently, the Cu/p-Sn catalysts exhibited a unique catalytic selectivity of high CO faradaic efficiency (FECO) of 58.1% at −1.0 VRHE, which cannot be obtained from the bulk Cu (FECO = 7.5%) and Cu/Sn catalysts without the Sn pattern (FEHCOOH = 90.6%). Moreover, the catalytic selectivity of the Cu/p-Sn catalysts shifted from CO to HCOOH as the thickness of the Sn pattern increased from 3 to 50 nm. This study sheds light on the origin of the local corrosion of bimetallic catalysts and its effect on the catalytic selectivity of CO2 reduction.

sections.text: KEYWORDS: Cu−Sn catalysts, bimetallic, carbon dioxide reduction, selectivity, galvanic corrosion, patterning

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) to value-added chemicals provides an appealing route for utilizing CO2 as an energy storage source.1,2 Among various CO2 conversion methods, the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2 RR) on a metal surface has attracted tremendous attention because the selection of an appropriate metal catalyst enables the controlling of the types of products such as carbon monoxide (CO),3−7 formate (HCOOH),8−13 alcohols, and hydrocarbons.14−16 Compared to the multicarbon products that suffer from significant reductive overpotentials and low selectivity, high faradaic efficiencies (FEs) and large production rates for single-carbon products, such as CO and HCOOH, provide more immediate opportunities for practical applications.17,18
Previously, metal catalysts were categorized into two groups based on their products: (1) Au, Ag, Pd, and Zn from which CO is the major product;3−7,19 (2) Pb, In, Sn, and Bi, preferentially producing HCOOH.8−13,20,21 Although almost all metal catalysts have catalytic properties for one product, Cu catalysts can change their selectivity of CO and HCOOH by alloying with other secondary metals. For instance, bimetallic Cu catalysts such as Cu−In,22−24 Cu−Sn,25−29 and Cu− Pd30−32 have been developed to increase the selectivity of CO
because the binding strength of CO* and H* can be weakened.24,33 The weakened binding strength of H* suppressed the hydrogen evolution reaction, and the decreased binding strength of CO* inhibited the further reduction of CO to hydrocarbons. As a result, a high faradaic efficiency of CO (FECO) up to 90% could be obtained. On the other hand, Cu− Bi,34−36 Cu−Au,37 and Cu−Sn38−41 bimetallic catalysts enhanced the selectivity toward formate (FEHCOOH > 95%) by stabilizing the adsorption of the OCHO* intermediate. Even though the Cu-based bimetallic catalysts could demonstrate the high selectivity of CO and HCOOH, fundamental challenges still remain for understanding the reasons for enhanced catalytic properties. For instance, Cu−Sn bimetallic catalysts, prepared through the coating of Sn nanoparticles (NPs) on Cu nanowires, resulted in FECO greater than 90%.26 However, Cu−Sn NPs fabricated by a chemical synthetic method showed high FEHCOOH > 70%. 38 In

short, fabrication and characterization methods are required to investigate the effect of each composition and geometry on the catalytic selectivity of bimetallic catalysts. Recently, the microfabrication of bimetallic Cu−In catalysts
has demonstrated the controlled variation of the geometry and composition to derive the correlation with catalytic performance and monitor the active phase.22 They explained that the active sites were spontaneously formed around the Cu/In interfaces via the solid-state diffusion of In species during the CO2 RR. Although they found that the spontaneously formed In-modified Cu catalyst increased the CO evolution activity, the mechanisms and driving forces for the changes in the morphology are still unknown. When two metals are in contact with each other in aqueous electrolytes, the galvanic corrosion reaction should be considered because the potential difference between the oxidation reactions acts as a driving force for the change in surface composition.42−44 However, changes in the morphology and catalytic performance of the Cu-based bimetallic catalysts induced by the galvanic corrosion reaction have not been studied in detail. Herein, we study the origin of the spontaneous corrosion phenomenon of bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts by experimental approaches based on photolithography and physical vapor deposition. The patterning of Sn layers on the Cu foil activates the local galvanic corrosion of Sn patterns during CO2 RR, thereby resulting in the thinning of Sn patterns. The corroded Sn sequentially migrated to the Cu foil and produced bimetallic Cu−Sn phases with a high Cu/Sn ratio. The Curich Cu−Sn catalysts showed a unique catalytic selectivity of high FECO = 58.1% at −1.0 VRHE, which cannot be obtained from the bulk Cu (FECO = 7.5%) and Cu/Sn catalysts without the Sn pattern (FEHCOOH = 90.6%). Moreover, we found that
the surface composition of Cu and Sn depends on the thickness of Sn patterns (tSn), leading to a gradual shift in the selectivity from CO to HCOOH as tSn increased from 3 to 50 nm.

sections.heading: 2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
sections.text:
2.1. Patterning of Sn Layers on Cu Foil. Purchased Cu foils (Nilaco) were electrochemically polished for 3 min in the H3PO4 solution (Samchun Chemical, 85%) by applying an anodic potential of 2.5 V versus the IrOx counter electrode. Then, the Cu foils were rinsed with deionized water and dried by N2 blowing. For the photolithography process, a photoresist (Micro Chemicals, AZ 5214) was spin-coated at 6000 rpm for 40 s and softly baked at 110 °C for 60 s. The photoresist-coated samples were transferred to a mask aligner (Karl Suss, MJB3), and a patterned photomask was contacted on the samples. The diameter of the patterns on the photomask was 3 μm. Ultraviolet light (wavelength = 280−450 nm) was illuminated on the samples through the photomask for 60 s, followed by immersing the samples in an MIF 400 developer for 90 s (Micro Chemicals). After photolithography, Sn layers were deposited by the thermal evaporation method under a base pressure of 1 × 10−6 Torr with a deposition rate of 0.1 nm/s. The rate and thickness of the Sn layers were in situ monitored by using a quartz crystal thickness monitor. An Sn pellet (99.99%, purchased from iTasco) was used as a source material. The lift-off process was conducted by immersing the sample in acetone for 5 min. For the Cu/Sn catalysts, thin Sn films with desired thicknesses were deposited on the electrochemically polished Cu foil by the thermal evaporation method. The catalysts were sealed with epoxy except for the active area of the electrodes (0.283 cm2) to prevent unwanted reactions at the backside and the edge of the Cu foil.
2.2. Characterizations. Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) were conducted using a PHILIPS XL30S FEG with an acceleration voltage of 5 kV and a working distance of 6 mm. X-ray diffraction (XRD)
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.0c01617 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
B
patterns were obtained from a diffraction meter (Rigaku, Dmax2500pc). High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) analysis were performed using a Cs-corrected JEM 2200FS operated at 200 kV. Cross-sectional TEM samples were fabricated using a focused ion beam system (SII SMI3050SE). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was measured using a Thermo ESCALAB250i X-ray photoelectron spectrometer at a base pressure of 10−9 Torr. The PHI 700 Scanning Auger Nanoprobe (3 keV, 10 nm) was used for Auger electron spectroscopy (AES). 2.3. Electrochemical Measurements. Linear-sweep voltammetry (LSV) measurements were conducted in an H-type cell separated by a nafion membrane with a three-electrode system using a potentiostat (Ivium Stat). Ag/AgCl filled with 3 M KCl was used as the reference electrode and Pt mesh was used as the counter electrode. The electrolyte used for electrochemical measurements was an aqueous solution of 0.1 M KHCO3 (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.95%) prepared by dissolving the solid salt in deionized water. The electrolyte was saturated with CO2 gas (99.99%) before the measurements were performed. The measured potential (VAg/AgCl) (V) could be converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (VRHE) (V) by using the Nernst function: VRHE = VAg/AgCl + 0.222 + 0.0592 × pH. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was measured in a frequency range from 1 MHz to 0.1 Hz at a potential of −1.0 VRHE with an amplitude of 30 mV. All measurements were conducted under ambient pressure at room temperature. 2.4. Product Analysis. Gas products were analyzed using a gas chromatographer (Inficon, 3000 Micro GC) equipped with two thermal conductivity detectors (TCD) connected to the Molsieve column and the Plot U column. Before beginning the electrochemical reduction, the apparatus was purged with CO2 gas for 3 min to remove other gases. During the reaction, gas was circulated within the reactor at a flow rate of 50 mL min−1. After the reaction, the gas products were automatically pumped into the gas chromatographer for analysis. The liquid product was analyzed using a 500 MHZ 1H 1D liquid nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrometer (Bruker) at 25 °C. The standard solution consisted of 5 mM dimethyl sulfoxide (Sigma-Aldrich) in D2O (Sigma-Aldrich) as a solvent. The amount of formate was calculated by integrating the areas of the products with that of the dimethyl sulfoxide standard solution. All catalysts were measured three times using a gas chromatographer and one time using an NMR spectrometer.

sections.heading: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
3.1. Morphology of Cu/Patterned-Sn Catalysts. Photolithography and physical vapor deposition methods allowed the bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts with a well-defined geometry and composition (Figure 1a). To pattern the Sn layer on the Cu foil, a photoresist was applied on the Cu foil and patterned with ultraviolet light, followed by developing circular regions (Figure S1). Then, the Sn patterns with the desired thickness were deposited by thermal evaporation (Figure S2), and the photoresist was lifted-off from the Cu foil. The detailed methods are described in the Experimental Section 2. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) images showed that the circular Sn patterns were successfully fabricated on the Cu foil (Figure 1b). The Cu element was distributed on the entire surface of the catalysts, whereas the Sn element existed only on the patterned regions. The electrochemical CO2 RR was conducted for the Cu foil/ patterned-Sn (Cu/p-Sn) catalysts with thin (3 nm) and thick (20 nm) Sn patterns in 0.1 M KHCO3 at −1.0 VRHE for 20 min. Before the CO2 RR, both thin (3 nm) and thick (20 nm) Sn patterns showed distinct boundaries with the Cu foil (Figure 1c,d). However, after the CO2 RR, thin Sn patterns (3 nm) changed the morphology from the circular to the distorted shape and the boundary with the Cu foil became
unclear (Figure 1c). On the other hand, the thick Sn patterns (20 nm) maintained their circular shape after the CO2 RR. (Figure 1d). We confirmed that this dramatic change in the morphology of the Sn pattern occurs only when the thickness of Sn (tSn) was less than 5 nm and within 20 s of the reaction (Figure S3). The change in the shape of the pattern was observed not only in CO2-purged electrolyte but also in N2purged 0.1 M KHCO3 (Figures S4 and S5), which means that this phenomenon is mainly originated from the reductive reaction in the electrolyte and not from the interaction between the catalyst and the absorbates such as *CO, *COOH, or *OCHO. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) analysis further evidenced that the change in the morphology depends on the thickness of the Sn patterns (Figure S6). In the Cu/p-Sn 3 nm electrode, the shape of the circular Sn pattern was distorted after the CO2 RR. However, no noticeable change in the surface geometry was observed in Cu/p-Sn 20 nm. Since the shape of the pattern was not clearly distinguished due to the rolling marks of the Cu foil, once more, we formed the Sn patterns on the extremely flat Cu substrate45 and performed the same reaction (Figure S7). The thickness contrast observed at the boundaries of patterns revealed that the Sn patterns have a concave shape with the border taller than the center. Although the shape of the Sn pattern is concave, it is evident that the size of the Sn patterns became smaller after the CO2 RR reaction on Cu/pSn 3 nm. Meanwhile, the circular Sn patterns were preserved in Cu/p-Sn 20 nm. These results indicate that the extent of change in the morphology during the reaction is highly dependent on the tSn.
3.2. Microstructure of Cu/Patterned-Sn Catalysts. We measured the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of Cu/Sn 20 nm and Cu/p-Sn 20 nm before and after the CO2 RR to investigate the microstructure of Cu, Sn, or the CuSn alloy (Figure S8). Regardless of the Sn pattern or the CO2 RR, all samples showed the Cu planes of (111), (200), and (220). There was no diffraction pattern from Sn or the CuSn alloy. Furthermore, the microstructure of Cu/p-Sn 3 nm was characterized using a cross-sectional transmission electron microscope (TEM) after the CO2 RR. It is apparent that the ∼3 nm-thick SnOx layer was formed on the Cu foil (Figure 2a). The high-resolution TEM image and the selected area electron diffraction patterns showed d-spacing values of 0.209 and 0.181 nm, which correspond to the Cu (111) and Cu (200) planes, respectively (Figure 2b). No crystal plane was detected in the SnOx layer, which indicates that the SnOx layer is the amorphous phase. The electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) elemental mapping of Sn (Figure 2c) and Cu (Figure 2d) revealed a distinct boundary between the Cu foil and the SnOx layer, confirming the bilayer structure without interdiffusion or alloying.
3.3. Surface Chemical Composition of Cu/PatternedSn Catalysts. To study the change in the chemical compositions, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was characterized. There was no clear difference in the intensity and bonding state of C 1s XPS spectra for all samples (Figure S9). This means that there is no photoresist residue, but the carbon species are adsorbed onto the surface during handling in the ambient laboratory environment. The Cu 2p3/2 XPS spectra were deconvoluted into the two peaks of metallic Cu− Cu (932.6 eV) and Cu−O (933.7 eV) (Figure 3a).46,47 The repeated oxidation and chemical etching processes of the Cu foil during electropolishing can leave oxides on the surface.
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.0c01617 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
C
However, all samples showed a high ratio of Cu−Cu to Cu−O greater than 5, indicating that the electropolished Cu foil mainly consists of Cu with a little amount of oxide. Because the catalytic activity of the thin copper oxide layer is indistinguishable from that of polycrystalline Cu,48 we can consider the electropolished Cu foil as a metallic Cu substrate. Before the CO2 RR, all catalysts showed a relatively weak intensity of the Cu 2p3/2 spectra because the photoelectrons emitted from Cu
foils were screened by the Sn layers. However, after the CO2 RR, the Cu/p-Sn 3 nm catalyst exhibited remarkably increased intensity of the Cu 2p3/2 spectrum. This result indicates that a large amount of Cu spontaneously presents on the surface during the CO2 RR. On the other hand, two samples of Cu/Sn 3 nm and Cu/p-Sn 20 nm catalysts showed little difference in the intensity of the Cu 2p3/2 spectra after the CO2 RR, indicating that the amount of Cu on the surface remained almost the same. Sn 3d5/2 XPS spectra were fitted into two peaks of Sn−Sn (484.9 eV) and Sn−O (486.5 eV) (Figure 3b).49,50 The Sn 3d5/2 spectra of Cu/Sn 3 nm and Cu/p-Sn 3 nm exhibited an intensive Sn−O peak with a small metallic Sn−Sn peak. The oxide peaks originated from native oxides (SnOx) formed during the exposure of the samples to the ambient air prior to XPS analysis. Interestingly, despite the dramatic change in the morphology of Cu/p-Sn 3 nm after the CO2 RR, the intensity of Sn 3d5/2 was nearly identical, indicating that the amount of Sn on the surface is retained. As a result, there was a remarkable difference in the atomic ratio of Cu and Sn (Figure S10). The Cu/p-Sn 3 nm catalyst exhibited a 2.81-fold increase in the Cu/Sn ratio after the CO2 RR, while Cu/Sn 3 nm and Cu/p-Sn 20 nm revealed 1.57- and 1.48-fold increase in the atomic ratio of Cu/Sn, respectively. From these results, we believe that the tSn of Sn patterns plays a critical role in the composition of the bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts because the Cu/Sn ratio changes over several nanometers away from the Cu/Sn interface during the CO2 RR. The high lateral resolution of the Auger electron spectroscopy (AES) elemental mapping allows the determination of the homogeneity of elements on Cu/p-Sn 3 nm before and after the CO2 RR (Figure 4). The as-prepared Cu/p-Sn 3 nm catalyst showed circular Sn patterns on the Cu foil (Figure 4a). It is noticeable that the Sn elements were only detected in the patterned region (Figure 4b), but the Cu elements were present on the whole surface (Figure 4c). In the patterned region, there were many O elements due to the formation of
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.0c01617 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
D
SnOx (Figure S11). The preferred oxidation of the Sn pattern is a piece of evidence of local corrosion, which occurs due to the difference in the oxidation potentials of Cu and Sn. After the CO2 RR, the morphology of the Sn patterns changed (Figure 4d). Simultaneously, the elemental distribution of Sn spread out of the patterns (Figure 4e). It is expected that an ultrathin Sn layer forms outside the pattern as the Sn patterns become thin. On the other hand, no significant change was observed in the compositional distribution of Cu (Figure 4f). To compare the amount of each element of Sn and Cu on spots 1−4, AES spectra were plotted (Figure 4g). The patterned region (spot 1) has high Sn composition (Sn/Cu = 1:3), and Sn was not detected at the outside of the patterns (spot 2). However, after the CO2 RR, the amount of Sn in the patterned region (spot 3) decreased (Sn/Cu = 0.85:3), and the AES spectrum of Sn was detected at the outside of the patterns (spot 4). These results prove that the Sn patterns became thinner and the Sn elements were simultaneously migrated to the outside of the patterns during the CO2 RR. 3.4. Electrochemical CO2 Reduction. To study the effect of Sn patterns on the catalytic activity toward the CO2 RR, four samples such as Cu foil, Cu/Sn 3 nm, Cu/p-Sn 3 nm and Cu/p-Sn 20 nm catalysts were evaluated. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) scans were measured in CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte at a scan rate of 50 mV/s (Figure S12). In all samples, the cathodic current density was the largest at the first scan and saturated after the second scan, indicating
that the native oxide layers were reduced during the first scan of LSV measurements. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were performed to quantify the kinetics of electron-transfer processes (Figure S13). The interprets of the Nyquist plot in the high-frequency region represent the solution resistance, and the following semicircle in the low-frequency region indicates the charge transfer resistance of the mass transfer during the electrochemical CO2 RR. The Cu/p-Sn 3 nm and the Cu/p-Sn 20 nm catalysts had smaller impedance arcs in the second semicircle than the Cu and the Cu/Sn 3 nm, indicating that the patterning of the Sn layer on the Cu foil reduced the charge transfer resistance. These results are consistent with those of LSV measurements where the measured current densities at −1.0 VRHE were − 1.23, −1.16, −1.89, and − 1.75 mA/cm2 for Cu, Cu/Sn 3 nm, Cu/p-Sn 3 nm, and Cu/p-Sn 20 nm, respectively. To find the reason for the increased current density of Cu/p-Sn catalysts, the electrochemical surface area (ECSA) was measured using the charge/discharge curves and the current densities were plotted at 0.52 VRHE as a function of the scan rate (Figure S14). Because the slope of the current density−scan rate curve indicates a double layer capacitance that linearly correlates with the ECSA, the active surface area of catalysts could be determined. All samples such as Cu, Cu/Sn 3 nm, Cu/p-Sn 3 nm, and Cu/p-Sn 20 nm exhibited the double-layer capacitances of 0.17, 0.11, 0.13, and 0.08 mF/cm2, respectively. The ECSAs of catalysts are similar, which means that the
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.0c01617 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
E
charge transfer kinetics is enhanced by the catalytic activity of the material rather than the surface roughness. The faradaic efficiencies (FEs) of Cu, Cu/Sn 3 nm, Cu/p-Sn
3 nm, and Cu/p-Sn 20 nm catalysts were measured at different applied potentials from −0.6 to −1.2 VRHE (Figure S15 and Table S1). The Cu foil mainly produced H2 at all potentials (FEH2 > 50%) and began to generate CH4 at high potentials (FECH4 = 34.8% at −1.2 VRHE). However, after deposition of a 3 nm thick Sn layer on the Cu foil (Cu/Sn 3 nm), the typical catalytic properties of Sn-like catalysts were obtained; H2 evolution was dramatically suppressed (FEH2 < 5.5%), and the selectivity of the formate was significantly increased (FEHCOOH > 80%) at high potentials (−0.8∼ −1.2 VRHE) (Figure 5a).11 Interestingly, the patterning of the thin Sn layer (tSn = 3 nm) on the Cu foil (Cu/p-Sn 3 nm) exhibited unique catalytic selectivity; FECO greatly increased to the maximum value of 58.1% at −1.0 VRHE (Figure 5b), and the maximum FEHCOOH was as low as 24.1% at −1.0 VRHE (Figure 5a). At the high potential of −1.2 VRHE, FECO decreased and FECH4 increased because the applied potential provided sufficient energy for the subsequent hydrogenation of CO to generate CH4. On the other hand, Cu/p-Sn 20 nm showed a little decreased FECO of 35.3% and increased FEHCOOH of 61.6% at −1.2 VRHE. The trends in the selectivity for HCOOH (Cu/Sn 3 nm > Cu/p-Sn 20 nm > Cu/p-Sn 3 nm > Cu) and CO (Cu/ p-Sn 3 nm > Cu/p-Sn 20 nm > Cu ≈ Cu/Sn 3 nm) show that the catalytic selectivity of bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts could be controlled by patterning. Also, the selectivity of the Cu/Sn and Cu/p-Sn catalysts depends more on the properties of the material (i.e., morphology and composition) than the potential in the range of −0.6 to −1.2 VRHE in which the electrochemical properties are generally evaluated in CO2 reduction.
To investigate whether the catalytic selectivity of bimetallic Cu−Sn is dependent on tSn, we measured the FEs of Cu/Sn (Figure 5c) and Cu/p-Sn catalysts (Figure 5d) for various tSn values (Table S2). Cu/Sn catalysts with tsn ≥ 2 nm exhibited a high FEHCOOH of >80% at −1.0 VRHE. However, the ultrathin Sn layer (tsn = 1 nm) showed a high FECO of 86.1%. This dramatic transition of catalytic selectivity at tsn = 1 nm is in good agreement with the previous result of Cu/SnO2 core/ shell NPs where the thick SnO2 shell (1.8 nm) showed selective formate production, whereas the NPs with the thinner (0.8 nm) shell are CO selective.51 In contrast to Cu/Sn catalysts, the Cu/p-Sn catalysts exhibited the transition of catalytic selectivity at much thicker Sn patterns at tSn = 5 nm. The samples with thin Sn patterns (2 nm ≤ tSn ≤ 4 nm) showed a high FECO of ≥51.2%. However, a further increase in tSn (> 5 nm) resulted in a marked decrease in FECO below 40% and an increase in FEHCOOH to 59.7%. Previously, the bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts are known to be selective for C1 products such as CO or HCOOH because the binding strength of both CO and absorbed hydrogen (H*) to the Cu substrate can be weakened by the incorporation of Sn.33 By decreasing the binding strength of H* on the Cu surface, the hydrogen evolution reaction is suppressed due to the lack of available sites at which H* can recombine with an electron. Also, decreasing the binding strength of CO on the surface of Cu inhibits the further reduction of CO to alcohols or hydrocarbons. It is generally accepted that CO and HCOOH are produced by parallel pathways, and the selectivity of each product is determined by the key intermediates of *COOH and *OCHO, respectively.52 Density functional theory showed that Sn donates electrons to Cu and is positively charged in the Cu−Sn alloys. Because the localized positive charges on the catalysts hinder the nucleophilic attack on the carbon and increase the
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.0c01617 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
F
thermodynamic barrier to *COOH adsorption, a pathway through the *OCHO intermediate is likely preferred rather than the *COOH intermediate. Thus, the bimetallic Cu−Sn catalyst with a high Cu/Sn ratio is selective for CO, whereas that with a low Cu/Sn ratio is selective for HCOOH production. Because the Cu/p-Sn 3 nm catalyst has a high Cu/Sn ratio resulting from the local corrosion of Sn patterns, its CO selectivity can be higher than that of Cu/Sn 3 nm or Cu/p-Sn 20 nm. From the results, we found two important facts that are required for the spontaneous formation of Cu/pSn catalysts for selective CO production: (1) both surfaces of Cu and Sn should be in contact with the electrolyte and (2) Sn patterns should be thin enough to obtain a high Cu/Sn ratio by the local corrosion reaction. We evaluated the stability of the Cu/p-Sn 3 nm and the Cu/ p-Sn 20 nm catalysts for 3 h at a constant potential of −0.8 VRHE in 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte (Figure S16a). The CO2 gas was continuously bubbled in the electrolyte to prevent the changing of the pH value during the reaction for the chronoamperometric measurement. The Cu/p-Sn 3 nm catalyst exhibited a nearly constant current density of ∼1.08 mA/cm2 at −0.8 VRHE and the Cu/p-Sn 20 nm catalyst also showed a current density of ∼1.13 mA/cm2, indicating stable electrical properties. For the faradaic efficiency measurements, the electrolyte was replaced with clean CO2-purged KHCO3 solution after the reaction for 1 h was completed to prevent the increase in the concentration of the products in the reactor. At the initial stage of the reaction (20 min), the Cu/p-Sn 3 nm catalyst showed an FECO of 56.8% and an FEHCOOH of 37.8%. However, these FEs of CO and HCOOH slightly decreased to 53.0 and 31.3%, respectively, after 3 h reaction due to increased FEH2 (Figure S16b). Similarly, the Cu/p-Sn 20 nm catalyst showed a high FEHCOOH of 48.5% and an FECO of 31.6% at a reaction time of 20 min (Figure S16c). However, FEs decreased to FEHCOOH = 46.5% and FECO = 25.6% after 3 h reaction. Although the FEs of CO and HCOOH decreased, the tendency of the Cu/p-Sn 3 nm catalyst to generate CO and that of Cu/p-Sn 20 nm to produce HCOOH are maintained even after 3 h reaction. 3.5. Local Galvanic Corrosion of Bimetallic Catalysts. In corrosion science, the patterning of a metal on the different metallic substrates can promote corrosion kinetics much faster than each pure metal due to the local galvanic coupling where one metal acts as the anode and the other as the cathode.53 In this manner, Sn corrodes faster than Cu when both Cu and Sn metals contact with each other in the oxidant environment because the potential difference between the oxidation reactions of Cu and Sn acts as a driving force. At the negative potential, the following reactions occur on the Cu region and patterned Sn:
+ + +− − −FeCO H O 2 HCOO OH2 2
+ + +− −F FeCO H O 2 CO 2OH2 2
+ +− −FH e2 O 4 H 2OH2 2 The resulting OH− increases the local pH near the surface.54 Since the Sn is electrochemically vulnerable to oxidation compared to Cu, the patterned Sn could be preferentially oxidized to oxide, hydroxide, or oxyhydroxide as the following equation:55
+ +− −Fy ySnO OH SnO (OH) ex x y
Simultaneously, these oxides could be reduced to metallic Sn during the CO2 RR. These complex and repeated redox reactions resulted in the thinning of Sn patterns and migration of Sn species (Figure 6). Although we could not clearly explain
the exact reaction pathways of Sn oxidation and migration at this moment, the patterned Cu−Sn would follow several major steps: anodic reaction at patterned Sn, cathodic reaction at the Cu foil, and migration. This local galvanic corrosion enormously increased the atomic ratio of Cu/Sn on both patterned regions and outside of the pattern when the Sn pattern was thin (tSn ≤ 5 nm). On the other hand, when the tSn is thick (> 5 nm), the bulk region of Sn is relatively stable and maintains the low Cu/Sn ratio. Therefore, Cu−Sn catalysts with a high Cu/Sn ratio selectively produce CO, but the production of HCOOH is favorable for catalysts with a low Cu/Sn ratio. To determine whether the driving force for the changes in the surface morphology is a difference in the oxidation potentials of two metals, we fabricated Sn and Ag patterns on Cu foil pieces using the thermal evaporation method through the shadow mask (Figure S17a). Interestingly, even in the large pattern size of 150 μm, local corrosion was observed in the circular region of Sn patterns (tSn = 3 nm) (Figure S17b). The morphology change was evident in the patterned Sn region, and the change was more pronounced at tSn = 3 nm than tSn = 50 nm (Figure S17c). In the case of Ag patterns on the Cu foil, the Ag patterns showed little change in the morphology after the CO2 RR, whereas small particles were spontaneously formed on the Cu region because of the repeated redox processes of Cu (Figure S17d). Based on the trend of the change in the morphology (Sn > Cu > Ag), we concluded that the local galvanic corrosion is the primary reaction mechanism for the change in the morphology of bimetallic catalysts. To date, many high-performance Cu−Sn catalysts have been demonstrated by various methods such as hydrothermal methods,56 coelectrodeposition,39 and chemical synthesis.57 Although the catalytic performance of Cu/p-Sn or Cu/Sn is not as good as the world record values (Table S3), this work has originality to investigate the reason for the changes in the surface composition and morphology of the bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts during the CO2 RR. We believe that the greater the difference between the oxidation potential of the two metals,

G
the faster the corrosion. Quantifying the potential difference required for corrosion in various bimetal combinations would provide a guideline to design a new bimetallic catalyst in the future.

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
In summary, we found the spontaneous change in the surface morphology and composition induced by local galvanic corrosion in bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts during the CO2 RR. When the thin Sn layer was patterned on the Cu foil, the Sn patterns were preferentially corroded due to the difference in the oxidation potential. Accordingly, the repeated redox reaction activated the thinning of Sn patterns and simultaneously the migration of Sn to the outside of the patterns. As a result, the Cu/p-Sn 3 nm catalysts exhibited the unique catalytic selectivity of a high CO faradaic efficiency (FECO) of 58.1% at −1.0 VRHE, which cannot be obtained from the bulk Cu (FECO = 7.5%) and Sn catalysts (FEHCOOH = 90.6%). Also, the thickness of the Sn pattern was found to play a critical role in the selectivity of CO2 RR. FECO shifted from 55.8 to 33.2%, and FEHCOOH gradually increased from 37.2 to 59.7% at −1.0 VRHE as the tSn increased from 2 to 20 nm. This work experimentally demonstrated that new catalytic properties could be realized through the local surface corrosion reaction of bimetallic catalysts.
